title: India–Pakistan

cards.h: The rivalry that shapes the neighbourhood
cards.b:
India–Pakistan is the most dangerous bilateral relationship in Asia: two nuclear-armed states, one unsettled territorial dispute (Kashmir), cross-border terrorism and a shared river system.

The topic is asked in many forms: Kashmir, terrorism, Indus Waters, nuclear stability, confidence-building measures and, since May 2025, Operation Sindoor and its aftermath.

A good answer shows the cycle: a terror attack, Indian retaliation, a crisis, third-party concern, then an uneasy calm. And it explains why talks have repeatedly failed to hold.

cards.h: Wars, accords and attempts at peace
cards.b:
The Simla Agreement (1972) (Indira Gandhi and Z.A. Bhutto) committed both to settle disputes bilaterally and to respect the Line of Control (LoC) of December 1971. India reads it as barring third-party mediation.

The Lahore Declaration (February 1999) was signed by Vajpayee and Nawaz Sharif. Months later Pakistan's army occupied heights in Kargil. India recovered them in a limited war, without crossing the LoC.

• India: J&K acceded legally by the Instrument of Accession (26 October 1947). The whole former princely state, including PoK and Gilgit-Baltistan, is Indian. Parliament's 1994 resolution says so.
  • Pakistan: Kashmir is 'unfinished business' of Partition. It points to UN Security Council resolutions (1948–49) on a plebiscite, and calls for self-determination.
  • Kashmiri voices: range from autonomy to independence. Many want to be part of any talks.

August 2019: India abrogated Article 370, split J&K into two Union Territories (J&K and Ladakh) and removed special status. The Supreme Court upheld this in In re: Article 370 (December 2023). J&K held assembly elections in 2024. Statehood restoration remained pending as of 2026.

Pakistan downgraded diplomatic ties and suspended trade in 2019.

India says the core problem is cross-border terrorism backed by Pakistan's army and intelligence (ISI). Key attacks: Parliament (2001), Mumbai 26/11 (2008), Pathankot (2016), Uri (September 2016), Pulwama (February 2019) and Pahalgam (22 April 2025).

  • 2016: after Uri, 'surgical strikes' across the LoC.
  • 2019: after Pulwama, an air strike at Balakot; Pakistan retaliated and an Indian pilot was captured and returned.
  • 2025: after Pahalgam (26 killed, mostly tourists), India launched Operation Sindoor on 7 May, striking nine sites linked to terror groups, then Pakistani military targets. Four days of drone and missile exchanges ended in an understanding on 10 May, reached through the DGMO hotline.

Modi laid down a new line: any terror attack will be treated as an act of war, no difference between terrorists and their sponsors, and no tolerance for 'nuclear blackmail'.

• 23 April 2025: India put the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, closed the Attari border post, cancelled visas, cut High Commission staff.
  • Pakistan's response: closed airspace to Indian airlines and suspended trade. It threatened to suspend Simla and other bilateral pacts.
  • Mediation dispute: Trump claimed credit for the ceasefire. India said no third party was involved. Pakistan thanked him.
  • Pakistan's military: Gen. Asim Munir was promoted Field Marshal in May 2025. Reports say Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia in September 2025.
  • Trade and travel: still frozen. Cricket contacts limited to multilateral events.

India calls Operation Sindoor 'paused', not over. The ceasefire has held on the LoC since May 2025, as of 2026, but there is no formal dialogue.

The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) was signed in 1960 at Karachi, mediated by the World Bank, by Nehru and Ayub Khan.

  • Eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) go to India.
  • Western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) go mainly to Pakistan. India may build run-of-river hydropower with design limits.
  • A Permanent Indus Commission, a Neutral Expert and a Court of Arbitration handle disputes (Kishenganga, Ratle).

India put the treaty in abeyance in April 2025. In August 2026 the Court of Arbitration at The Hague, in an award India refused to attend, held that the treaty remains in force and cannot be suspended by one side. India rejected the award, calling the court illegally constituted, and maintains that the abeyance continues until Pakistan ends support for terrorism. A Neutral Expert decision on Ratle is expected around mid-2027. Pakistan calls any water stoppage an 'act of war'.

cards.h: Nuclear deterrence and the stability-instability paradox
cards.b:
Both states tested weapons in 1998 (India 11 and 13 May; Pakistan 28 May). India follows no first use and 'credible minimum deterrence'. Pakistan has no no-first-use pledge and a 'full spectrum deterrence' with short-range Nasr missiles.

Glenn Snyder (1965) described the stability-instability paradox: nuclear weapons make big wars unlikely, but make smaller conflicts safer to start. Pakistan's use of terrorists under a nuclear shield fits this idea. India's response was limited, conventional, calibrated strikes that show resolve but stay under the nuclear threshold (Cold Start debate, surgical strikes, Balakot, Sindoor).

Existing CBMs: the 1988 agreement not to attack nuclear facilities (lists exchanged every 1 January), the 2005 pre-notification of ballistic missile tests and the DGMO hotline.

Doves cite the 2003 ceasefire and 2004–07 Composite Dialogue, when Kashmir violence fell. Hawks argue that every opening was followed by an attack, from Lahore to Kargil and Pathankot to Pulwama.

The current Indian line, in the words of the Foreign Ministry, is that talks and terror cannot go together, and that if talks are held they will be on terrorism and PoK. Pakistan wants to discuss Kashmir and water.

cards.h: What India can and cannot do
cards.b:
Can: isolate Pakistan diplomatically (FATF grey-listing in 2018–22), keep up military pressure, build water infrastructure on the western rivers, and shape UN debates.

Cannot easily: change Pakistan's army-driven policy, or stop China's backing (J-10C and PL-15 supplies, CPEC, UNSC shielding).

Good practice for answers: link Pakistan with the China factor, the US factor (Trump–Munir), Afghanistan (the Taliban-Pakistan clashes since 2025–26 give India an opening) and domestic Kashmir politics (Omar Abdullah became J&K Chief Minister in October 2024).

"Cross-border terrorism and the Indus Waters Treaty: how should India respond?" (typical)
"India's relations with Pakistan: has the policy of 'talks and terror' reached a dead end?" (typical)
"Examine the nuclear dimension of the India-Pakistan rivalry." (typical)

Structure: (1) wars and agreements: Tashkent, Simla, Lahore; (2) Kashmir and Article 370; (3) terrorism and crises: Mumbai, Uri, Balakot, Sindoor; (4) IWT and the 2025–26 legal contest; (5) nuclear risk (stability-instability); (6) way forward: deterrence, backchannel, CBMs, no third-party mediation.

quiz.q: The Simla Agreement was signed in:
quiz.w: Indira Gandhi and Bhutto signed it on 2 July 1972.

quiz.q: Who signed the Indus Waters Treaty in 1960?
quiz.w: Nehru and Ayub Khan signed it in Karachi, with the World Bank also a signatory.

quiz.q: Under the IWT, which rivers are allotted mainly to India?
quiz.w: The three Eastern rivers: Ravi, Beas, Sutlej.
7 May 2025, after the Pahalgam attack of 22 April.

quiz.q: The Lahore Declaration was signed in:
quiz.w: February 1999 by Vajpayee and Nawaz Sharif.

quiz.q: The Supreme Court judgment upholding the abrogation of Article 370 came in:
quiz.w: In re: Article 370 of the Constitution, December 2023.

quiz.q: How was the May 2025 ceasefire reached, according to India?
quiz.w: India says the DGMOs agreed on 10 May 2025 over the hotline.

quiz.q: Pakistan's stated nuclear policy differs from India's in that Pakistan has:
o: No pledge of no first use
quiz.w: Pakistan keeps the option of first use under 'full spectrum deterrence'.

quiz.q: The 1988 India-Pakistan agreement on nuclear facilities provides for:
o: No attack on each other's nuclear installations
quiz.w: It bars attacks on nuclear installations; lists are exchanged each 1 January.
